questions.topic: The radial free-body diagram
questions.learningObjective: State what is absent from the radial diagram
questions.stem: An astronomer's log asks why centrifugal force does not appear in the radial free-body diagram of a satellite.

answer.exemplar: In an inertial frame centrifugal force is fictitious and does not act on the satellite; only real forces like gravity appear.

questions.explanation: Free-body diagrams in an inertial frame include only real forces. Centrifugal force appears only in rotating frames.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Period of a low circular orbit
questions.learningObjective: Explain how period depends on radius
questions.stem: An astronomer's log asks why the period of a low circular orbit increases with radius.

answer.exemplar: Period T=2*pi*sqrt(r^3/GM), so as radius grows the period grows as r^(3/2).

questions.explanation: The period depends on r^(3/2), so a larger orbit takes disproportionately longer to complete.
questions.hint: Recall T is proportional to r^(3/2).

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Only one speed gives a circular orbit
questions.learningObjective: State the condition for a circular orbit
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer asks for the condition that defines a circular orbit.

options.text: Gravitational force exceeds centripetal force.
Gravitational force equals centripetal force.
Centripetal force exceeds gravitational force.
options.misconception: thinks extra inward force is needed

options.text: No force is needed in space.

questions.explanation: A circular orbit requires gravity to supply exactly the centripetal force mv^2/r, fixing a unique speed.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why a moon breaks up before landing
questions.learningObjective: Explain the Roche limit in words
questions.stem: An astronomer's log asks for a plain-language statement of why a moon breaks up before landing.

answer.exemplar: A moon breaks up before landing because the planet's gravity pulls harder on its near side than its far side, tearing it apart at the Roche limit.

questions.explanation: The differential pull across the moon's diameter exceeds its self-gravity at the Roche limit, causing disruption.

questions.learningObjective: Identify when scale reading equals mg
questions.stem: An astronomer's log asks under what condition a scale reads exactly mg.

options.text: When the object is in free fall.
options.misconception: thinks free fall gives mg reading

options.text: When speed is zero.
When acceleration is zero.
When altitude is zero.

questions.explanation: Newton's second law gives N=m(g-a), so N=mg only when a=0. Speed can be nonzero.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Only one speed gives a circular orbit
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequence of wrong speed
questions.stem: An astronomer's log asks what happens if a satellite's speed differs from the circular speed at its radius.

answer.exemplar: If the speed is too low the satellite falls inward; if too high it moves outward, and the orbit becomes elliptical or escapes.

questions.explanation: Only the circular speed balances gravity and centripetal force; other speeds change the orbit shape or lead to escape.
questions.hint: Compare the speed with circular speed.

questions.stem: A table lists field 8.2 at the near end and 8.1 at the far end of a spacecraft; what does this imply?

options.text: The far end feels a stronger pull, compressing the craft.
The near end feels a stronger pull, creating a tidal stretch.
Both ends feel the same pull, so no stress occurs.
The difference is due to the craft's own mass.
options.misconception: attributes the field to the craft

questions.explanation: The near end is closer to the planet and feels a stronger field, producing a tidal force that stretches the craft.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Centre of mass of three masses
questions.learningObjective: Compute COM for a symmetric set
questions.stem: Masses 3 kg, 5 kg and 3 kg sit at -4 m, 0 m and 4 m; what is their centre of mass?
questions.explanation: x_cm=(3*-4+5*0+3*4)/(3+5+3)=0/11=0 m. Symmetry places the COM at the origin.
questions.hint: Use the weighted average of positions.
